lines: Two buyers want your shops, worth about six hundred sixty thousand dollars. A bike chain offers seven hundred thousand. A private equity firm offers six hundred sixty thousand, mostly with borrowed money.
Buyers usually pay more than today's value to take control. That extra is the control premium. For public companies, it's often twenty to forty percent above the share price.

The chain can pay more because of synergies: it saves twenty thousand dollars a year running your shops with its own. At six times, that's worth one hundred twenty thousand. So the most it should pay is seven hundred eighty thousand.
The private equity firm is a financial buyer. It does a leveraged buyout: it borrows sixty percent, three hundred ninety six thousand, and puts in two hundred sixty four thousand of its own money.

Over five years, the shops' cash pays the loan down to one hundred ninety six thousand. If EBITDA grows to one hundred forty thousand, the shops sell for eight hundred forty thousand, and the firm keeps six hundred forty four thousand.

That's a MOIC of two point four four times, about a nineteen and a half percent IRR. With no debt, it would be only one point five eight times. But if EBITDA falls to seventy thousand, the firm gets back only eighty five cents per dollar.

Debt cuts both ways. Toys R Us was bought with heavy debt in two thousand five and went bankrupt in two thousand seventeen. So use the private equity bid to push the chain toward seven hundred forty thousand.
